questions.question: What does a file editor in Linux allow you to do?

options.text: Create, view, and modify text files

explanation.correct: File editors in Linux allow you to create, view, and modify text files from the command line.
explanation.why: A is incomplete — editors do more than view. C is wrong — command-line editors only handle text files. D is incomplete.

questions.question: Which command opens a file called 'report.txt' in the nano editor?

explanation.correct: The correct syntax is simply: nano filename — so nano report.txt.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are not valid Linux command syntax for nano.

questions.question: What happens when you run 'nano newfile.txt' and the file does not exist?

options.text: An error is shown — you must create the file first
Nano creates the file and opens it for editing
Nano opens an empty unnamed buffer

explanation.correct: If the file does not exist, nano automatically creates it and opens it for editing.
explanation.why: A is wrong — nano handles file creation. B and D are incorrect behaviors.

questions.question: In nano, which key combination do you press to exit the editor?

explanation.correct: Ctrl + X exits nano. If there are unsaved changes, nano prompts you to save.
explanation.why: Ctrl + S is a Windows/GUI shortcut. Esc is used in vi/vim. Ctrl + Q is not a standard nano command.

questions.question: What does 'vi' stand for?

explanation.correct: vi stands for Visual Editor — it was the first screen-based text editor for Unix.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are not the correct expansions of vi.

questions.question: What does 'vim' stand for?

explanation.correct: vim stands for Vi IMproved — it adds features like syntax highlighting and multi-level undo on top of vi.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are not correct expansions.

questions.question: When you first open a file with vi, which mode are you in?

explanation.correct: Vi always opens in Command Mode by default. You must press 'i' to switch to Insert Mode before typing.
explanation.why: A is wrong — if you could type immediately, you'd be in Insert Mode, but vi doesn't work that way. B and D are not the default.

questions.question: How do you enter Insert Mode in vi from Command Mode?

explanation.correct: Pressing 'i' from Command Mode switches to Insert Mode, where you can type and edit text.
explanation.why: Enter does not change modes. : enters Last Line Mode. Ctrl+I is not used for mode switching.

questions.question: In vi, what indicator appears at the bottom of the screen when you are in Insert Mode?

explanation.correct: The -- INSERT -- indicator appears at the bottom of the vi screen when you are in Insert Mode.
explanation.why: A, B, and C are not the standard vi indicator text.

questions.question: How do you save and quit a file in vi?

options.text: Press Esc then type :wq and press Enter

explanation.correct: To save and quit: press Esc to go to Command Mode, type :wq (colon, w, q), then press Enter.
explanation.why: Ctrl+S is a GUI shortcut. :save is not a valid vi command. /save is a search pattern, not a save command.

questions.question: Which vi command quits WITHOUT saving?

explanation.correct: :q! force-quits vi without saving any changes. The ! overrides the safety check.
explanation.why: :w saves without quitting. :q quits but only if there are no unsaved changes. :wq saves and quits.

questions.question: What does the wc command stand for?

explanation.correct: wc stands for word count — it counts lines, words, and characters in a file.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are not the correct meaning of the wc command.

questions.question: You run 'wc report.txt' and see the output: 15 200 1500 report.txt. What does 200 represent?

explanation.correct: The three wc numbers are in order: lines, words, characters. So 200 is the word count.
explanation.why: 15 is lines (first number). 1500 is characters (third number). wc does not output file size in KB.

questions.question: Which wc option counts only the number of lines in a file?

explanation.correct: wc -l counts only lines. Think of -l as 'lines'.
explanation.why: -w counts words. -c counts characters/bytes. -n is not a wc option.

questions.question: What does 'grep' do by default with respect to case sensitivity?

options.text: It ignores case — matches ERROR, error, and Error equally
It is case-sensitive — searching for 'error' does not match 'Error'
It converts everything to uppercase before searching
It depends on the file type

explanation.correct: By default, grep is case-sensitive. 'error' will not match 'Error' or 'ERROR'. Use -i to make it case-insensitive.
explanation.why: A describes grep -i behavior. C and D are incorrect.

questions.question: Which grep option makes the search case-insensitive?

explanation.correct: grep -i makes the search case-insensitive, matching 'error', 'Error', 'ERROR', etc.
explanation.why: -c counts matches. -r searches recursively. -n shows line numbers.

questions.question: You want to search for the word 'timeout' in ALL files inside the /var/log directory and its subdirectories. Which command is correct?

explanation.correct: grep -r performs a recursive search, going through all files in the specified directory and all its subdirectories.
explanation.why: A would only search a single file or produce an error for directories. -n shows line numbers. -l lists filenames only.

questions.question: What does 'sort' do to the original file by default?

options.text: Permanently sorts and overwrites the original file
Sorts the file and saves a backup
Displays sorted output on screen but does not modify the original file
Creates a new file called sorted.txt automatically

explanation.correct: By default, sort only displays the sorted output on screen. The original file remains unchanged unless you use -o to redirect.
explanation.why: A is wrong — sort never overwrites unless explicitly told to. B and D are incorrect default behaviors.

questions.question: Which sort option removes duplicate lines from the output?

explanation.correct: sort -u sorts the file and removes duplicate lines from the output. The -u flag stands for 'unique'.
explanation.why: -r reverses the sort order. -n sorts numerically. -d is not a standard sort option for deduplication.

questions.question: What is the pipe symbol in Linux?

explanation.correct: The pipe symbol is | (vertical bar). It takes the output of one command and feeds it as input to the next.
explanation.why: & runs a process in the background. > redirects output to a file. // is not a Linux operator.

questions.question: What does the command 'cat /var/log/syslog | grep error | wc -l' do?

options.text: Displays all error lines from syslog
Counts how many lines in syslog contain the word 'error'

explanation.correct: The pipe chains three commands: cat outputs the file, grep filters only error lines, and wc -l counts those filtered lines.
explanation.why: A would be just wc -l syslog. B would be just grep error syslog. D is completely wrong — these commands are read-only.

questions.question: In vi, how do you navigate to the very last line of a file while in Command Mode?

explanation.correct: In Command Mode, pressing G (uppercase) moves to the last line of the file.
explanation.why: End is a GUI/shell shortcut. gg (lowercase) goes to the FIRST line. $ goes to the end of the current line, not the file.

questions.question: Which vi navigation key moves the cursor UP one line?

explanation.correct: In vi Command Mode: h=left, l=right, j=down, k=up. k moves the cursor up.
explanation.why: j moves down. h moves left. l moves right.

questions.question: You want to sort a file numerically in descending order (largest number first). Which command is correct?

explanation.correct: sort -nr combines -n (numeric sort) and -r (reverse order), giving numeric sort in descending order.
explanation.why: -n alone sorts numerically in ascending order. -r alone reverses the default alphabetical sort, not numeric. -d is not a standard option for this.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between nano and vi/vim in terms of operation model?

options.text: Nano only works on text files; vi/vim can edit binary files
Nano uses a single editing mode with visible shortcuts; vi/vim uses three distinct modes
Nano requires root privileges; vi/vim does not
Nano saves automatically; vi/vim never auto-saves

explanation.correct: The key difference is modes. Nano has one mode — you always type freely. Vi/vim has three modes (Command, Insert, Last Line), and understanding them is critical to using it correctly.
explanation.why: A is wrong — both handle text files. C is wrong — neither requires root by default. D is incorrect behavior.

questions.question: A developer runs 'sort fruits.txt -o sorted.txt'. What is the result?

options.text: fruits.txt is sorted in place and renamed to sorted.txt
The sorted content is written to sorted.txt; fruits.txt is unchanged
An error occurs because -o is not valid
Both files end up with unsorted content

explanation.correct: The -o option writes the sorted output to the specified file (sorted.txt) while leaving the original (fruits.txt) completely unchanged.
explanation.why: A is wrong — the original is not modified or renamed. C is wrong — -o is valid. D is incorrect.

questions.question: You are in vi Insert Mode and want to go to the beginning of the file without exiting and reopening. What is the correct sequence?

explanation.correct: First press Esc to leave Insert Mode and return to Command Mode, then type gg to jump to the beginning of the file.
explanation.why: :gg is not a valid Last Line command. Ctrl+Home and Home key are GUI shortcuts that don't work reliably in vi.

questions.question: Which grep command shows line numbers alongside the matching lines?

explanation.correct: grep -n prepends each matching line with its line number in the file, useful for quickly locating the exact position of a match.
explanation.why: -i ignores case. -l lists only filenames with matches. -r searches recursively.

questions.question: On an EC2 instance, you want to find all unique IP addresses in an access log and count how many there are. Which pipeline achieves this?

explanation.correct: grep filters lines with IP addresses, sort -u removes duplicates, and wc -l counts the remaining unique lines. This is a classic pipe chain.
explanation.why: A counts total IP mentions including duplicates. B counts all lines not just unique IPs. D pipes wc output into sort which is backwards.

questions.question: Which statement about vi/vim is correct from an AWS/cloud perspective?

options.text: vi/vim is optional — most EC2 instances have a GUI editor
vi is available on virtually all Linux systems including EC2 instances because it is POSIX standard
AWS recommends nano over vi for EC2 instance management
vi/vim requires a separate installation on Amazon Linux AMIs

explanation.correct: vi is included in the POSIX standard and is pre-installed on virtually every Linux/Unix system, including all AWS EC2 Linux instances. It is always available even on minimal installations.
explanation.why: A is wrong — EC2 instances are headless servers with no GUI. C is not an AWS recommendation. D is wrong — vi is pre-installed.

questions.question: In the context of Linux file editing, what does 'case-sensitive' mean?

options.text: The editor requires you to use the Shift key
Commands and searches treat uppercase and lowercase letters as different
File names can only be in uppercase
The editor only works with uppercase text

explanation.correct: Case-sensitive means uppercase and lowercase are treated as different characters. 'nano' is not the same as 'Nano' or 'NANO'.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are incorrect definitions of case sensitivity.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the -v option in grep?

options.text: Shows lines that do NOT match the pattern

explanation.correct: grep -v inverts the match — it shows all lines that do NOT contain the specified pattern. Useful for filtering out known good lines and focusing on the rest.
explanation.why: A would require --version. B is not what -v does in grep. D is not a grep behavior.

questions.question: What vi command takes you to line number 25?

explanation.correct: In Last Line Mode, typing :25 and pressing Enter moves the cursor to line 25. This is the standard vi syntax for jumping to a line.
explanation.why: goto, go25, and 'line 25' are not valid vi commands.

questions.question: You have a file with 5 identical lines 'apple'. After running 'sort -u file.txt', how many lines appear in the output?

explanation.correct: sort -u removes duplicate lines, so five identical 'apple' lines become one unique line in the output.
explanation.why: 5 would be the result without -u. 0 is wrong — there is one unique value. File size is irrelevant.

questions.question: Which command in nano saves the file without exiting?

explanation.correct: Ctrl + O (Write Out) saves the file to disk without exiting nano, allowing you to continue editing.
explanation.why: Ctrl+X exits nano. Ctrl+S is a GUI shortcut not native to nano. Ctrl+W opens the search function.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the pipe operator?

options.text: It can only connect two commands
It saves output to a file
It chains multiple commands, feeding each output as the next input
It runs commands in parallel simultaneously

explanation.correct: Pipe chains any number of commands together, passing each command's output as the input to the following command in sequence.
explanation.why: A is wrong — you can chain many commands. B describes output redirection (>). D is incorrect — commands run in a pipeline sequence.

questions.question: What happens if you try to quit vi with :q when there are unsaved changes?

options.text: Vi quits and discards changes silently
Vi shows a warning and does not quit until you save or force quit
Vi creates a backup file and then quits

explanation.correct: If there are unsaved changes, :q shows an error message and refuses to quit. You must use :wq to save and quit, or :q! to force quit without saving.
explanation.why: A describes :q! behavior. C is auto-save behavior which vi doesn't do by default. D is not standard vi behavior.

questions.question: In a pipe chain 'cmd1 | cmd2 | cmd3', in what order do the commands execute?

options.text: Right to left — cmd3 first, then cmd2, then cmd1
All three run simultaneously in parallel
Left to right — cmd1 first, its output feeds cmd2, which feeds cmd3

explanation.correct: Pipe executes left to right. cmd1 runs and produces output; that output becomes cmd2's input; cmd2's output becomes cmd3's input.
explanation.why: A is wrong — order matters and it is left to right. B is technically close (Linux starts them nearly in parallel) but conceptually the data flows left to right. D is wrong.

questions.question: You want to search all files recursively in the /home/user/projects directory for the text 'TODO'. Which command is correct?

explanation.correct: grep -r (recursive) searches through all files in the specified directory and all its subdirectories.
explanation.why: A without -r would fail on a directory or only check the directory itself. -l lists filenames but doesn't do recursive search alone. find is a different command.

questions.question: What is the most likely reason a student tries to type in vi and sees navigation keys moving the cursor or deleting text instead?

options.text: The student is in Command Mode instead of Insert Mode

explanation.correct: Vi's Command Mode interprets keypresses as navigation and edit commands. Letters like h, j, k, l move the cursor. You must press 'i' to enter Insert Mode before typing text.
explanation.why: A and B are not the typical cause. D is completely wrong — vi is a text editor.

questions.question: Which command saves sorted output from fruits.txt into a new file called sorted-fruits.txt?

options.text: Both A and B are valid ways to achieve this

explanation.correct: Both > (output redirection) and -o (output file option) save the sorted result to a new file. Both are valid and produce the same result.
explanation.why: A alone works. B alone works. D uses -s which is not the correct option for this.

questions.question: Why is vi/vim particularly important for AWS cloud engineers compared to nano?

options.text: AWS only supports vi, not nano
vi is POSIX standard and available on every Linux system — including minimal EC2 instances where nano may not be installed
vi runs faster on cloud infrastructure
AWS billing is lower when using vi

explanation.correct: vi is guaranteed to be present on any POSIX-compliant Linux system. Minimal EC2 AMIs may not include nano. A cloud engineer who only knows nano may be stuck on a minimal server.
explanation.why: A is wrong — both can be installed. C and D are irrelevant factors.

questions.question: What does 'wc -c filename.txt' count?

explanation.correct: wc -c counts the number of characters (bytes) in the file.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are not what -c represents in the wc command.
